title: Common Pitfalls
intro: The mistakes that cost the most time when building spiking columns, each as symptom → cause → fix, so you can recognise them from a raster plot.

blocks.text: Most failures of spiking column models are not exotic. They come from a small set of causes — the balance between excitation and inhibition, missing homeostasis, numerical integration, units and bookkeeping — and they show up as recognisable patterns in a raster plot or a rate histogram. Learn the patterns, and look at a raster before any accuracy number every time you change the model.

widget.title: What a layer looks like without inhibition

blocks.text: Things to try: with inhibition set to none, most excitatory cells fire for every input pattern, so the pattern SDRs overlap heavily and carry little information about which pattern is present — the dense, unspecific activity behind several pitfalls below. Switch to E/I feedback and then k-WTA and watch the active fraction and the overlap between patterns fall. Then, with E/I feedback, set the inhibitory gain to 0 and raise it step by step to see how much inhibition is needed before activity becomes sparse.

items: Runaway excitation. Symptom: rates climb to hundreds of Hz, limited only by the refractory period; the raster turns solid. Cause: recurrent excitation too strong relative to inhibition, often after STDP potentiated recurrent synapses. Fix: strengthen or speed up inhibition, bound weights, add weight normalisation or a net-depressive STDP window, and keep recurrent excitatory synapses plastic only once the rest is stable.

Silent network. Symptom: no or almost no spikes after the first few hundred ms. Cause: external drive below rheobase, thresholds that keep rising (adaptive threshold without decay), or a unit mistake that makes weights 1,000× too small. Fix: check a single neuron's input current against its rheobase; give adaptive thresholds a decay; print weights with units.

Synchronous bursts or oscillations. Symptom: vertical stripes in the raster; the population rate swings between zero and a high peak. Cause: inhibition too slow or too weak, delays all identical, or input that is too synchronous. Fix: faster inhibitory synapses (a few ms), heterogeneous delays and parameters, Poisson rather than regular input.

Inhibition too slow to compete. Symptom: k-WTA does not produce k winners — many cells fire before the inhibition arrives. Cause: inhibitory delay or time constant comparable to the time excitatory cells take to reach threshold. Fix: make inhibition faster than excitation, or let predicted/strongly driven cells reach threshold earlier, which is exactly how timing-based competition works in HTM-style spiking columns.

Dead and greedy units. Symptom: a few neurons win almost every input; many never fire. Cause: no homeostasis; early winners get stronger weights and win more. Fix: adaptive thresholds (Diehl & Cook 2015), boosting or intrinsic plasticity, weight normalisation; check the usage histogram after every training run.

All neurons learn the same feature. Symptom: identical receptive fields. Cause: missing or too-weak lateral inhibition, so all neurons learn from every input. Fix: stronger competition (k-WTA or soft WTA) during learning.

Weights saturate at the bounds. Symptom: a bimodal weight histogram piled at 0 and w_max, receptive fields lose detail. Cause: additive STDP is known to produce bimodal weights (Song, Miller & Abbott 2000). Fix: multiplicative or soft-bounded STDP (van Rossum et al. 2000), lower learning rates, normalisation.

Learning forgets old patterns. Symptom: earlier sequences or objects are no longer predicted after new training. Cause: learning rates too high, decrements applied to segments that should be left alone, or capacity exhausted. Fix: smaller decrements, learn only on segments that were active or matching, add cells or segments, and test retention explicitly.

Wrong input code for the rule. Symptom: STDP layer learns nothing useful; temporal memory never predicts. Cause: dense or non-overlapping encodings, or rate codes fed to a rule that expects precise timing (or the reverse). Fix: see "Encoding Schemes" and check the input overlap structure first.

Time step too large. Symptom: rates or learning change when you halve dt; spikes cluster on step boundaries. Cause: forward Euler with dt comparable to the fastest time constant, or Poisson probabilities r·dt that approach 1. Fix: dt of 0.1 ms for dynamics checks (1 ms is often acceptable for LIF networks once validated), exact integration for linear subthreshold dynamics where the simulator supports it, and always run a dt-halving check.

Order-of-update artefacts. Symptom: results depend on whether you update neurons or synapses first. Cause: a spike influences other neurons in the same step it is emitted, effectively a zero delay. Fix: use a minimum synaptic delay of one time step and a fixed update order.

Unit mistakes. Symptom: everything is off by factors of 1,000. Cause: mV vs V, nA vs pA, ms vs s, Hz vs per-ms rates. Fix: a simulator that checks units (Brian2), or a units column in your config file and asserts on derived quantities such as rheobase.

Unreproducible results. Symptom: a result cannot be recovered a week later. Cause: unseeded randomness, unrecorded parameters or library versions. Fix: seed everything, save the config and versions with every result, and report over several seeds.

Evaluating only on MNIST. Symptom: good accuracy, but the model cannot do anything column-specific. Fix: add sequence prediction, anomaly detection and sensorimotor recognition tests (see "Evaluating a Column").

Too much biological detail too early. Symptom: hundreds of parameters, nothing works, nothing can be debugged. Fix: start with LIF neurons and abstract segments; add detail only when a specific question needs it.

Hardware surprises. Symptom: the model works in the simulator and fails on the chip. Cause: weight and state quantisation, fan-in limits, missing support for the learning rule or for dendritic nonlinearities, different noise. Fix: simulate the hardware's constraints (fixed-point weights, limited fan-in) in software before porting, and compare spike statistics, not only task accuracy.
